lines: She gave you the Crest? Roxen doesn't hand those out, she loses them on purpose.
So you made her work. Good. Somebody should.
Now do me one. Next time somebody official asks what's under my quarry, tell me.
West working's stopped. Not unsafe, exactly. Just wrong.
Nineteen years I worked that face alongside Roxen and it never sounded hollow.
It sounds hollow now. Put your ear on it and tell me I'm imagining that.
Four thousand people in this city cut stone and about eleven of us still do.
Rest are on the tramway, or the sheds, or the Foundation.
Nobody starves. It's just strange, walking a street full of people
who've never had their hands on the thing the street is made of.
You came up out of her hole with a Crest on you. That's a first this year.
There's a stopped working at the west end, if you're feeling strong.
Nobody's been in there since the shift walked out.
Sleepers stay, rails go. That's how a working shuts: quietly, over about four years,
and everybody keeps saying next spring right up until nobody says it.
Mind your feet on those. They're older than your mother.

sw_bothy_kid: I can lift a stone THIS big.
...I can push a stone this big.
Pushing is lifting sideways. Dad says that's not how it works. Dad is wrong.

lines: Four down this month. One up. You.
The board goes up on the Hall door at noon and the whole terrace comes to read it.
That is how much there is to do in Stonewake. Enjoy it, it lasts a day.
You want the Hall? Sign here, and then go down. Down, not in.
There was a lad through here yesterday with the same look on his face.
He went down cheerful and he came up not cheerful. Learn from that or don't.
You want the Hall? Sign here, and then go down. Down, not in.
Keeper Quill keeps her Hall at the bottom of the old workings.
She has been asked to move it upstairs eleven times. Eleven.
I told you the weather on the ridge does as it pleases. I would like that back, please.
Ramp road is shut above the second bend. Not the stone. The wind. I have never shut it for wind.
Whatever you are going north for, go the long way round and eat something first.
Two Crests. Kerb Street east, then, and the coast road after that.
It is a long walk and the weather on the ridge does as it pleases.
Eat something before you go. That is not advice, that is an order.
Ramp road behind me, up to the terrace: quarry works and the Stone Hall.
Down there: Kerb Street, the market, the clinic on the corner.
Museum and the Foundation are on the north square. Don't get lost. Everyone gets lost.
First time? You'll be looking at the roofs. Everybody looks at the roofs.
Nine thousand four hundred, last count, and the count is always out.
Ramp road up to the Hall. Kerb Street for everything else.
South out of that gate is Route 2, and Briarbell a good day beyond it.
You came up that way? Then you know it's mostly forest and one very old arch.
People go and look at the arch. I've never once heard anyone say what it's for.
Lower Market. Sixty stalls on a good day, and the good days are Thursdays.
Anything off this mountain, anything off that road, and lately
a great deal from further off than either. Coast goods. Cheap, too.
Somebody's paying for the carriage and it isn't the seller.

sw_market_kid: Dad says don't talk to trainers because you'll want one.
I've been feeding a Gravelet behind the stall for a month. Don't tell him.
It's called Brick. It doesn't answer to Brick. It doesn't answer to anything.

lines: Have you been in? Good. Go back. There's a case at the far end
with eleven things in it I have not been able to explain in thirty years,
and a young woman standing at it who has explained four of them to me this week.
Free on the first of the month, which is not today, but come in anyway.
You look like somebody who has been outdoors. We collect those.
Half the good donations came in off the road in muddy boots.
Congratulations on the Crest. Genuinely - the whole office heard about it.
If you're going east, do call in at our Tideglass rooms.
Dr Veyl is there this season. He likes meeting people who actually walk the region.
Good afternoon. Do go in - the office is open to anyone, there's a display,
and there is usually tea if you look like you have walked a long way.
We are the Meridian Foundation. Weather, water, and Kin. Mostly weather.
The cistern went over the lip on Tuesday and it has not stopped going over since.
Down Kerb Street, into the market, and the market is on a slope so you can watch it choose.
Four inches down in the spring and nobody thought it was a question. It is a question now.
The cistern's been on the square since before the terrace was cut.
Fed off the mountain. Never dry, never once in living memory.
It went down four inches in the spring and came back up in a week.
Nobody could tell me why. Nobody even seemed to think it was a question.
I light them going up and the wind has them out again before I am four lamps on.
So I have stopped. Nobody has ever seen this city dark and nobody is thanking me for it.
Come out at dusk anyway. You can see the whole of it, and there is nothing to see.
Three hundred and forty lamps between the gate and the terrace.
I light them going up and I put them out coming down and in between
I am the only person in Stonewake who sees the whole of it lit at once.
It is worth the walk. Come out at dusk and stand on the ramp.
The clinic's free, you know. Everywhere. Whole region.
Some people go their whole lives not quite believing that
and stand out here working out what the catch is.
There you are! Right. Two things.
One: the Foundation office has thrown me out twice and I have questions.
Two: Roxen Quill put me on the floor of her own mine. Twice. In one day.
